title: How would you diagnose connection pool exhaustion in production?
description: Find leaked or held-open connections, understand MaxPoolSize behavior, and fix the patterns that starve the pool.

data.text: Connection pool exhaustion shows up as intermittent 'The pool has been closed' or 'Timeout expired' / 'Too many user connections' errors that appear under load and vanish when traffic drops. Every ADO.NET/EF connection comes from a small, shared pool — by default SQL Server caps at 100 connections per pool string. When consumers open connections and return them slowly (or never), new callers wait for the wait timeout and then fail. The symptom is a latency cliff followed by errors, even though the database server itself looks idle.

The interviewer is testing whether you can separate 'the database is overloaded' from 'we stopped getting connections'. Pool exhaustion is usually an application-lifetime bug — a held connection, a sync-over-async block, or a pool-per-connection-string multiplication — not a capacity problem on the server.

items: Correlate the timing: errors spike while SQL Server's own request queue stays shallow — check sys.dm_exec_sessions / sys.dm_exec_connections counts versus the app's error rate.

Narrow the pool: each distinct connection string (even trailing spaces or case differences) creates its own pool — a template string built with string interpolation can silently create thousands of tiny pools.

Trace open/close behavior: EF Core logging for 'Executed DbCommand' connection opens, or SqlConnection stats in .NET (AppContext switch 'Switch.Microsoft.Data.SqlClient.EnableTrace' style diagnostics).

Check for connections opened but never disposed: long-running requests that hold a connection while doing HTTP calls, lazy-loading inside a using block that spans a network call, or an open reader blocking the connection's return.
Watch the waiters: ADO.NET waits up to ConnectionTimeout (default 15s) for a free connection — rising latency with a hard 15s ceiling is the classic signature.
Watch for sync-over-async: Task.Result / .Wait() on database calls blocks thread-pool threads; as threads starve, connections are held longer, and the failure cascades.

data.text: Code: the leaks that cause it

data.title: Connection lifetime mistakes in C#
Who is holding connections
data.code:
-- Active sessions and their wait types
SELECT s.session_id, s.status, s.login_name, s.host_name,
       s.wait_time, s.wait_type, c.connect_time, t.text
FROM sys.dm_exec_sessions s
LEFT JOIN sys.dm_exec_connections c ON c.session_id = s.session_id
OUTER APPLY sys.dm_exec_sql_text(c.most_recent_sql_handle) t
WHERE s.is_user_process = 1
ORDER BY s.wait_time DESC;

-- Pool pressure signals: high WAIT on lock or async network IO on the server
-- while pool waits never reach SQL Server -- that gap IS the diagnosis
SELECT COUNT(*) AS sessions FROM sys.dm_exec_sessions
WHERE is_user_process = 1;

-- If sessions are low while the app reports pool timeouts,
-- the bottleneck is client-side pooling, not the database.

data.title: Pool waits are invisible to the database
data.text: Connections stuck waiting for a pooled connection never reach SQL Server — server dashboards stay green while the app fails. If the database looks calm and the API is timing out at a consistent ~15 seconds, look at the client pool first, not the query plans.
Fixes that hold up under load

items: Tight scopes: open as late as possible, dispose always (await using), never hold a connection across HTTP calls or user I/O.
One pooled string per topology; fix string-comparison drift ('Pooling' differences split pools).
Tune Max Pool Size deliberately — raising it helps only if the database can actually serve more concurrent queries; otherwise it just moves the queue.
Set a short Connect Timeout (3–5s) so callers fail fast and shed load instead of stacking 15s waiters.
Keep everything async: sync-over-async is the most common way one slow request starves everyone.
Bulk work gets its own dedicated connection/settings (SqlBulkCopy, separate pool) so it cannot drain the request path's pool.
Alert on pool wait time and errors alongside database CPU — they fail in different places.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Calm database + consistent ~15s client timeouts = pool starvation, not slow queries.
Held-open connections, sync-over-async, and interpolated connection strings are the classic causes.
Each distinct connection string is its own pool — template strings multiply pools.
Fix lifetimes and go fully async before raising Max Pool Size.
data.takeaway: Connection pools fail client-side while the server stays green: tighten connection lifetimes, eliminate sync-over-async, and only then tune pool sizes.
